rationale: A wins because it gets one more real protagonist on the board: "Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack instead of building it" is a usable retailer-strategy angle, and the line "It only works if a grocer is in the story" keeps it from becoming fantasy. B is clean, but "Over 6,000 brands now advertise on a grocery-delivery app — what that says about retail media" is the safer, more obvious ad-trade lane and leaves the make-versus-buy story untouched. Both are above the usual mush; A gives the founder more doors without pretending the risky one is already nailed shut.
gaps_in_A: "Instacart's delivery growth has stalled" overstates the supplied fact. "Slowed to single digits" is not the same as stalled.
"The checkout line is quietly disappearing from a few hundred grocery stores" is punchier than the evidence allows. A few hundred Caper deployments do not prove checkout lines are disappearing.
"Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack instead of building it" turns partnerships into a make-versus-buy thesis. It is a good angle, but it needs a named grocer before it is safe.
gaps_in_B: "Over 6,000 brands now advertise on a grocery-delivery app" narrows the ad business to an app surface. The facts say ads come from 6,000 brands, not where every ad runs.
"delivery growth has stalled to single digits" sharpens the fact past the evidence. Single-digit growth is slowing, not necessarily stalled.
"the move by retailers to sell ads against their shopper data rather than make money on the goods themselves" imports a broad retail-media thesis and shopper-data claim not supplied in the update.
B leaves the 1,500-retail-banner fact mostly as context. That misses a separate retailer-strategy angle about grocers outsourcing commerce, ads, and store tech.
